title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
editorial_summary: Use a dynamic sliding window tracking the most recent index of each character to expand right and jump left forward.

hints.tier1: Notice that any duplicate character invalidates the current substring. We only need to check if the next character has already appeared in the active window.
hints.tier2: Dynamic Sliding Window with Hash Map: maintain left pointer and map of `char -> last_seen_index`.
hints.tier3: If `s[right]` is in the map and `last_seen[s[right]] >= left`, jump `left = last_seen[s[right]] + 1`.
hints.tier4: Edge case: empty string `""` returns 0; string with all unique characters; string with all identical characters.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
editorial_summary: Store prefix sum frequencies in a map. Subarray (i...j) equals K when prefix[j] - prefix[i] == K.

hints.tier1: Since numbers can be negative, standard sliding window does not work because prefix sums are non-monotonic.
hints.tier2: Transform the problem into Prefix Sums: sum(i...j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]. If this equals K, then prefix[i-1] = prefix[j] - K.
hints.tier3: Maintain a hash map of running prefix sum counts. At each index, add `counts.get(curr_sum - k, 0)` to the total answer.
hints.tier4: Crucial: initialize `counts = {0: 1}` so that subarrays starting exactly at index 0 are counted.

title: Koko Eating Bananas
editorial_summary: Binary search on eating speed K in range [1, max(piles)]. Feasibility check computes hours required in O(N).

hints.tier1: If Koko can finish with speed K, she can definitely finish with any speed > K. The answer space has a strict monotonic boundary.
hints.tier2: Binary Search on Answer Space: range is `[1, max(piles)]`.
hints.tier3: Predicate `can_eat(speed)`: sum of `ceil(pile / speed)` across all piles. If `hours <= h`, feasibility is True.
hints.tier4: Ceil division without floats: `(pile + speed - 1) // speed` to avoid precision issues.

title: Daily Temperatures
editorial_summary: Maintain a monotonic decreasing stack of indices. Pop when current temperature is strictly higher than stack top.

hints.tier1: For each day, you need the nearest future day that is strictly warmer. Brute force is O(N^2), but earlier colder days are resolved by warmer days.
hints.tier2: Monotonic Decreasing Stack storing day indices.
hints.tier3: While `temperatures[i] > temperatures[stack[-1]]`, pop index `prev` and set `ans[prev] = i - prev`.
hints.tier4: Indices left in stack at the end have no warmer future day, so default answer is 0.

title: Network Delay Time
editorial_summary: Standard Dijkstra from starting node K. Answer is max(dist) across all nodes if all are reachable, else -1.

hints.tier1: Signal travels simultaneously along all wires. The time when all nodes receive the signal is the maximum of the shortest times from K to each node.
hints.tier2: Dijkstra's shortest path with Min-Heap `(time, node)`.
hints.tier3: Maintain `dist` initialized to infinity. Discard stale entries when `d > dist[u]`.
hints.tier4: If any node remains unreachable (`dist[i] == inf`), return -1; 1-indexed node IDs.

title: Course Schedule
editorial_summary: Determine if directed dependency graph has cycles using Kahn's algorithm or 3-color DFS.

hints.tier1: Taking course A requires course B. Can all courses be finished? This is equivalent to asking: is the directed graph acyclic (a DAG)?
hints.tier3: Calculate in-degrees. Enqueue all nodes with in-degree 0. As you process, decrement in-degree of neighbors. Count how many courses were processed.
hints.tier4: If processed count equals total numCourses, return True; otherwise False (cycle present).

title: Solve The Maze
editorial_summary: Greedily block all neighbors of bad people with walls. Then run BFS from exit (n,m) to check reachability of good people.

hints.tier1: Instead of checking each person separately, block the Bad people by surrounding them immediately with walls.
hints.tier2: Greedy + Reverse BFS from exit `(n, m)`.
hints.tier3: If any Good person is adjacent to a Bad person, it's impossible. Block all 4 adjacent cells of every Bad person. Then run BFS backwards from the exit.
hints.tier4: Verify that no Bad person can reach the exit, and all Good people can reach the exit.

title: Boredom
editorial_summary: Aggregate counts into count[x]. If you pick x, you gain x*count[x] points but cannot pick x-1. Equivalent to House Robber.

hints.tier1: Picking element X deletes all occurrences of X-1 and X+1. But picking X lets you take ALL occurrences of X for free!
hints.tier2: Dynamic Programming similar to House Robber: reduce the problem to frequency array `count[x]`.
hints.tier4: Array values up to 10^5, answer can exceed 32-bit integer (use 64-bit int / long long in C++).

title: Sum of Two Values
editorial_summary: Find two array elements with sum equal to target X. Return 1-based indices.

hints.tier1: Sort pairs `(value, original_index)` or use a hash map `val -> index`.
hints.tier2: Two Pointers on sorted array or Hash Map lookup.
hints.tier3: If sorted: `left = 0, right = n-1`. If `sum < X`, `left++`; if `sum > X`, `right--`.
hints.tier4: 1-based indexing required by CSES; output 'IMPOSSIBLE' if no pair exists.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
editorial_summary: Maintain smallest ending tails with binary search in O(N log N).

hints.tier1: O(N^2) DP is simple with `dp[i] = max(dp[j] + 1)`. But can we do better? At any length K, what is the best ending element to keep?
hints.tier3: Maintain `tails` where `tails[i]` is the smallest tail of all increasing subsequences of length `i+1`. Use `bisect_left`.
hints.tier4: Duplicate values: strictly increasing requires `bisect_left` to overwrite equal values.

title: Range Sum Query - Mutable
editorial_summary: Implement mutable range sum queries in O(log N) using a Fenwick Tree or Segment Tree.

hints.tier1: Regular array has O(1) update and O(N) query. Prefix sums have O(N) update and O(1) query. A balanced structure gives O(log N) for both.
hints.tier2: Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick) or Segment Tree.
hints.tier3: Fenwick Tree with 1-based indexing using `i += (i & -i)` for updates and `i -= (i & -i)` for prefix sums.
hints.tier4: Updating an element: pass delta `new_val - old_val` to `bit.update(idx, delta)`.

title: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array
editorial_summary: Insert numbers into a 0-1 Trie. For each number, greedily choose opposite bit from MSB to LSB.

hints.tier1: To maximize bitwise XOR, you want the highest bits (MSB) to be 1 as much as possible.
hints.tier3: For each bit from 31 down to 0, check if child `1 - current_bit` exists. If yes, add `1 << bit` to the answer and traverse that branch.
hints.tier4: Prefix set approach can also be used in O(32 * N).
